text: Incident management exists to minimize the negative impact of incidents by restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible. That's the ITIL 4 purpose statement, word for word. An incident is any unplanned interruption to a service, or a reduction in its quality — a report that won't load, a terminal that freezes, an email server running slow. The job here is restoration, not diagnosis. A workaround that gets the service running again counts as a full success, even if nobody yet knows why it broke.

Every incident starts as a logged record: what broke, who reported it, which service is affected, and when. Categorization sorts it by type so it reaches the right resolver group fast. Then comes prioritization, where impact and urgency meet. Impact asks how much damage this is doing — one user inconvenienced, or an entire branch offline. Urgency asks how fast it needs fixing. Together, those two factors decide queue position and who gets paged first.

ITIL 4 describes two models for getting the right expertise onto an incident. Tiered escalation is traditional: first-line handles what it can, and passes harder issues up one level at a time. Swarming instead pulls multiple people together at once — first-line, specialists, sometimes a vendor — working the same incident together from the start. Swarming trades some efficiency for speed and shared context when the cause isn't obvious yet. Organizations increasingly blend both models.

A major incident carries the highest category of impact — a wide outage, a safety issue, serious reputational risk — and runs under its own faster-moving process. That usually means a dedicated incident manager coordinating the response, a bridge call pulling in every team that might be needed, and much more frequent stakeholder communication, even before anyone has a fix. The normal queue-and-prioritize flow is simply too slow when the business is bleeding visibly.

The distinction that trips people up most: incident management is not responsible for finding out why something broke. If a restart or a known workaround gets users working again, the incident is resolved, full stop. Figuring out the deeper cause belongs to a different practice entirely — problem management, exactly where this chapter heads next.
